Executive Summary This report highlights the critical need for advanced modeling of data centers due to their rapidly increasing energy consumption and their impacts on power grid reliability. Driven by the demand for artificial intelligence (AI) applications, data centers are projected to consume a significant portion of U.S. energy by 2028, stressing an already challenged grid. This paper emphasizes the importance of “fast” timescale models to understand the dynamic interactions between data centers and the grid, especially given the rapid power fluctuations of AI workloads. It outlines a modeling framework that includes both offline and real-time electromagnetic transient domain simulations, detailing the necessary representations for various components, such as utility interfaces, transformers, information technology loads, uninterruptible power supply, cooling loads, battery energy storage systems, generators, protection systems, and higher-level control systems. Although standard simulation tools like PSCAD offer basic models, custom development is often required to accurately capture the unique and fast-changing behaviors of modern data centers. The paper also discusses key metrics and test cases for validating these models, focusing on transient load responses, protection relay coordination, and demand flexibility. Finally, it addresses the challenges of modeling large-scale data centers, such as computational complexity and the trade-off between model fidelity and practicality, suggesting hybrid modeling approaches as a solution. The overarching goal is to create a robust framework that helps assess data center impacts on grid stability, identify vulnerabilities, and inform the development of standards for these reliable integration of these large loads into the bulk power system. iv This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications.
